text: You may have already forgotten me, but I will remind you of some circumstances, and I believe you will remember who I am. Do you remember when you were traveling through Europe, you had also stopped in Prague, and all the Bulgarian students treated you so coldly, even Jireček, and only I was the one who invited you to my home and you stayed overnight for several days? Do you remember when you found me with the landlady’s daughter? And do you remember when you were left alone, how they treated you to food and you sang to them “The Night Is Terrible”? I am the same one, Bodkov; I have already completed my higher education and have returned to my fatherland. Since among my acquaintances I have no other influential person besides you, I turn to you with a request and ask you to ask one of the editorial offices of some government newspaper to print the enclosed letter, of which I am also sending you a copy, in case it should get lost at the editorial office. I believe that this letter is sufficient for the government to form an idea of my views; I am even able to write much more than this, if the need arises. I have graduated in philosophy, Mr. Balkanski! Besides that, I have one request to make of you: my father is a contractor, and now they are rejecting fifty thousand leva worth of shoes for him, so I will ask you to intercede so that they accept them, just as they accepted from the same material from a Jew. Is that patriotic?

Do not think that I am writing my article to please the government. Not at all. The discarding of the shoes has nothing to do with the article, and at last you should know that I am not a man who trades in his convictions.
Please accept the assurance of my highest esteem.
P. S. The editorial staff may alter my contribution as they see fit; I am not a pretentious person.
P. P. S. The shoes were discarded three days ago.
Here is the article referred to in the above letter:

My blood runs cold in my veins, my brain stiffens against my skull, my heart ceases to beat, and with trembling of my soul I cry out to the Honorable Government and beg it to answer: will there be an end to its patience toward the destructive unbridledness of the opposition press? The people want to know (I can boldly affirm this) when the sacrilegious fingers of the opposition, which dare to touch - oh, horror! - the Virgin and Sacred Person of our common Father, the pledge of our happiness and prosperity, will be broken. Instead of a submissive, reverent bow before the bright embodiment of our independence, instead of a kneeling readiness to satisfy the Most High lusts and desires, there appear among us Bulgarians (degenerates of the Bulgarian people) who dare to ascribe human weaknesses to the untouchable Person!!!... This is more than a betrayal of the interests of the fatherland. This is a debauchery unprecedented in history! There even appeared such brigands of the pen who rose up and tried to stop and defile the greatest virtue of our municipalities, where they donate municipal forests, islands, and gardens to their Most High Favorite. The greatness of the throne is at the same time the greatness of the people, and instead of being proud that our municipalities visibly demonstrate their love for the Crown and the Dynasty, instead of rejoicing that our until recently wild fatherland is covered with splendid palaces and villas, there are Bulgarians - imagine, Bulgarians! - who are not satisfied even after that! Such malcontents sow debauchery in society, and the Bulgarian people must look upon them with disgust. They are the cause of the moral decline of our society and of that distrust which is instilled between the government and society and so badly affects the people's livelihood. From this distrust suffer the private interests of the most respected and conscientious merchants, as is the case with our highly esteemed citizen NN, to whom these days, by mistake, shoes made of the finest material worth 50,000 leva were condemned. And so, the Government must take measures to shut the mouths of the opposition once and for all. This is the hottest desire of the Bulgarian people.
I promise you henceforth to write to you as many such articles against the opposition as you wish; I will only ask that my name remain anonymous to the public. I have finished with philosophy.

It comes to my mind who you were, Your Grace; how could I not remember? I remember you, and I remember your fiancée, and her mother was a *zararsaz*; didn’t I teach them how to cook this and that, and we used to play the piano too, I remember very well.

You have learned the trade, as I see you; this philosophy, it seems, was not meant only to bring out fools. And as for the shoes you write about, you have made a small mistake: that matter does not get settled with a note. You see, the Jew you mention had his shoes accepted—indeed they were accepted—because he knows where Abraham digs roots; so you too, loosen your purse strings.

I read your letter from beginning to end and understood what your trouble is, but to be an entrepreneur is not a spoonful for every mouth; it does not resemble philosophy, and you must figure out for yourself on whom it depends whether your shoes will be accepted, that is, on your father.

And as for what you say about the dynasty, well, let it go on; that is the fashion now. After all, a word does not make a hole.

I am addressing you, as you are a народен representative, and we ask that in the future such things not be repeated, where an entire regiment goes into the forest and barks like dogs, and the officers beat hares, because we were not sent to learn how to bark, but to defend our fatherland, and completely exhausted, worn out, with tears running from your eyes, hungry, and they force you to bark, and it must be done well, like a hound, otherwise you get beaten because you did not know how to bark like a hunting dog, and they killed only five (5) hares. It is a good thing they did not injure some soldier, because he would again get beaten for not having taken care. Besides that, they appointed me as an orderly, and I wash the child’s little trousers, and the python’s too, I do. This is a shameful thing, and we ask you to issue a law, and since I have nothing more to write to you, I remain. Tear up the letter.

Aren’t you Trъпko Komita’s son? I know your father. As for what you say, that they made you bark at rabbits in the forest, I heard that too, but patience is salvation, as that fellow said, one does not kick against the pricks. After all, we endured under the Turks our whole lives; what is it to endure under Bulgarians for two years? It’s no great matter. And as for the little underpants, it’s not a good thing for a man; that’s women’s work, but what can you do—wash the underpants and turn your head away, politics requires it that way. You know what they are like, but you just blink and endure, and greet your father, don’t forget. Patience, nothing else; these things are sorted out with patience, not with uproar. A submissive head, you know, the sword does not cut it.

I want to send our Rada abroad to study this year, and so that there won’t be any expenses, I beg you to act there before the bigwigs so that they may assign me on some mission, to study certain questions or for some agitation: for example, I could study the question of getting our homespun cloth introduced for the Belgian army, or study in Switzerland the ethnography of the Kutzo-Vlachs, or something similar. If they want, they can invent ninety-nine missions. I am even willing to accept three napoleons a day. Reply to me as soon as possible.

P. S. You too will not remain without benefit from this business trip. If they ask you about my education, tell them that although I do not have a diploma, I have read a great deal, and it is as if I have a higher education.
I could not find an answer to this letter in Bay Ganyo’s notebook, but in the envelope I found a draft of the following telegram:
You are very late, Vasile; someone else, more learned than you, has already been assigned to these matters.

Man proposes, but God disposes: all the plans we had made for my future have been shattered to dust. My career is utterly ruined. I have been expelled from school and am doomed to three years’ servitude in the convict companies, and the cause of it all is that cursed Bulgarian orthography: lately a new fashion has appeared, to write foreign words and names as they are supposedly pronounced, e.g. not to write minister, but ministăr, not to write ansambl, but ansamblŭ, not to write Bokl, but to write Bokăl, because this was supposedly more in keeping with the Bulgarian language, as though the nature of our language were to draw itself inevitably toward Afghan. We opposed our learned instructors, and they declared us rebels. On the very day of the Nativity of Jesus Christ, the Savior of mankind, under a mounted gendarme escort, we, unwilling pedestrian tourists, were driven along the snowy roads of Mother Bulgaria, and we march, march from stage to stage, sleep at the stations, bailiffs receive us, gendarmes see us off, and where they are taking us, we ourselves do not know. They say that, in order to make Bulgarian orthography triumph, they have found it useful to educate us for three years in the convict companies. Who knows! Perhaps this wonder too will come to pass. I have now been brought here, to your town, and I am writing this letter from the prison room. If you please, come and see me, and bring a doctor, because I do not know whether it is from the journey or from the cold, but these days I have begun to spit blood.

P. S. I have heard, uncle, that the Turks had a custom on the great holidays, such as Christmas and Easter, to release Christian prisoners on bail so that they could see their loved ones and spend the holy days. Is that true, uncle?

What you were looking for, uncle, that’s what you found. Who’s to blame? I wonder how they didn’t give you a good beating on top of that. Of course. Are we playing with walnuts here, or running a kingdom? What kind of freedom is this? What are you babbling to me about the Turks, that they were more merciful? They are not merciful, but fools. If they were smart, they wouldn’t give their kingdom to someone else. If you ask me, I’m glad, indeed, that at last they’ve got hold of you properly. Go now and wander through the police stations and barracks, so that you come to your senses, so that you remember when you were sticking your head up. I could not understand from your letter what the reason was; you write to me about some Bòkŭl - Mòkŭl, but I don’t believe you, even though I don’t understand grammar. Who knows what mischief you have done again. I have no time to go around the police stations and compromise myself before the great men by meeting with rebels. How many times have I taught you that a bowed head is not cut by a sword. You did not listen to me — now break your own head. What you were looking for, uncle, that’s what you found.
